title: Mathematical Area Atlas
subtitle: The sub-disciplines of mathematics, characterized by the property they encode and the operation they enable.
intro: Mathematics as a map of areas. Each area is characterized by the property it encodes or represents and the operation it enables; the essences are conceptual signatures, not formal definitions.

families.name: Foundations
families.essence: The languages and rules that make mathematical reasoning possible.

families.name: Quantity
families.essence: Number and measure: quantitative properties and the operations that combine them.

families.name: Structure
families.essence: Operations, symmetries, and the laws they obey.

families.name: Space
families.essence: Spatial properties, from figures and coordinates to continuous deformation.

families.name: Change
families.essence: Limits, accumulation, and the representation of change.

families.name: Chance
families.essence: Uncertainty, inference, and decision under incomplete information.

families.name: Computation
families.essence: Effective procedures, approximation, and extremal search.

families.name: Methods
families.essence: Cross-cutting ways of proceeding that cut across the areas.

areas.name: Logic
areas.essence: The form of valid inference: what follows from what, independent of content.
areas.description: Logic studies the form of valid inference. It asks which conclusions follow from a set of premises by virtue of their structure rather than their content, and it supplies the rules of proof, consistency, and satisfaction used across mathematics.

areas.name: Set Theory
areas.essence: Collections and membership: the foundational encoding of mathematical objects.
areas.description: Set theory encodes mathematical objects as collections and membership. It provides the vocabulary of sets, functions, relations, and cardinality, and it supplies the universe in which the other areas build their structures.

areas.name: Category Theory
areas.essence: Structure represented by objects and morphisms, with composition as the primitive.
areas.description: Category theory represents mathematical structure through objects and morphisms. Composition, functors, and natural transformations let it compare constructions across areas without depending on their internal representation.

areas.name: Type Theory
areas.essence: Propositions and proofs encoded as types and terms.
areas.description: Type theory encodes propositions and proofs as types and terms. It provides a foundational language in which computation and deduction share a syntax, and it underlies proof assistants and typed programming languages.

areas.name: Model Theory
areas.essence: Theories and their models: truth across structures.
areas.description: Model theory studies theories and their models. It compares structures by the sentences they satisfy and the mappings that preserve them, connecting syntax, semantics, and algebraic structure.

areas.name: Arithmetic
areas.essence: Quantitative properties encoded as numbers, plus the operations that combine and compare them.
areas.description: Arithmetic encodes quantitative properties in numeral systems and operates on them. It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation, together with the rules that govern them.

areas.name: Number Theory
areas.essence: Properties of integers and their arithmetic relations: divisibility, primes, congruences.
areas.description: Number theory studies the integers and their arithmetic relations: divisibility, primes, congruences, and the distribution of integer solutions. It is arithmetic pursued for the structure of number itself rather than for calculation.

areas.name: Algebra
areas.essence: Operational structure encoded symbolically, independent of particular values.
areas.description: Algebra encodes operational structure symbolically. It replaces particular numbers by variables and studies the laws that operations satisfy, so that the same reasoning applies across different domains.

areas.name: Linear Algebra
areas.essence: Vector spaces and linear maps: superposition, basis, dimension, eigenstructure.
areas.description: Linear algebra studies vector spaces and linear maps. It supplies the language of basis, dimension, superposition, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors, and it underlies geometry, analysis, and computation.

areas.name: Abstract Algebra
areas.essence: Groups, rings, fields, and modules classified by their laws and symmetries.
areas.description: Abstract algebra classifies algebraic structures — groups, rings, fields, modules — by their operations and laws. It studies symmetry, composition, and the morphisms that preserve structure.

areas.name: Representation Theory
areas.essence: Symmetry represented by linear actions on vector spaces.
areas.description: Representation theory represents abstract symmetry by linear actions on vector spaces. It turns group and algebra elements into matrices, making structural questions accessible to linear algebra.

areas.name: Geometry
areas.essence: Spatial properties represented as figures, configurations, and transformations.
areas.description: Geometry represents spatial properties as figures, configurations, and transformations. It studies incidence, distance, angle, curvature, and the invariants that survive a change of viewpoint.

areas.name: Analytic Geometry
areas.essence: Spatial properties recoded as coordinates and equations, turning geometry into algebra.
areas.description: Analytic geometry recodes spatial properties as coordinates and equations. Points become tuples, curves become equations, and geometric relations become algebraic conditions.

areas.name: Algebraic Geometry
areas.essence: Geometric objects represented as solutions of polynomial equations.
areas.description: Algebraic geometry represents geometric objects as solutions of polynomial equations. It connects the algebra of rings and ideals with the geometry of varieties, schemes, and their morphisms.

areas.name: Differential Geometry
areas.essence: Spatial properties represented through local linear structure, curvature, and connection.
areas.description: Differential geometry represents spatial properties through local linear structure. Manifolds, tangent spaces, connections, and curvature describe shape and motion without a fixed ambient coordinate system.

areas.name: Topology
areas.essence: Spatial properties invariant under continuous deformation: connectivity, holes, boundary.
areas.description: Topology studies spatial properties invariant under continuous deformation. It classifies spaces by connectivity, holes, boundary, and the existence of continuous maps rather than by metric distance.

areas.name: Algebraic Topology
areas.essence: Topological spaces studied through algebraic invariants.
areas.description: Algebraic topology studies topological spaces through algebraic invariants. Homology, cohomology, and homotopy groups translate topological questions into algebraic ones.

areas.name: Trigonometry
areas.essence: Angular and periodic relations represented by ratios and circular functions.
areas.description: Trigonometry represents angular and periodic relations through ratios and circular functions. It connects triangle geometry, oscillation, and the geometry of the circle.

areas.name: Order Theory
areas.essence: Comparison and ranking represented by partial orders, lattices, and bounds.
areas.description: Order theory represents comparison and ranking through partial orders, lattices, and bounds. It studies what it means for one element to precede another, and the structures that make comparison coherent.

areas.name: Combinatorics
areas.essence: Discrete configurations counted, arranged, and compared.
areas.description: Combinatorics counts, arranges, and compares discrete configurations. It studies permutations, combinations, graphs, and the principles that enumerate or bound finite structures.

areas.name: Graph Theory
areas.essence: Pairwise relations represented as vertices and edges.
areas.description: Graph theory represents pairwise relations as vertices and edges. It studies connectivity, paths, cycles, colouring, and the structure of networks.

areas.name: Tensor Analysis
areas.essence: Multilinear relations represented by components that transform under change of basis.
areas.description: Tensor analysis represents multilinear relations by components that transform under a change of basis. It supplies the language of stress, curvature, and field equations in geometry and physics.

areas.name: Analysis
areas.essence: Change and accumulation represented through limits, continuity, and approximation.
areas.description: Analysis represents change and accumulation through limits, continuity, and approximation. It makes precise the ideas of convergence, derivative, integral, and the behaviour of functions.

areas.name: Real Analysis
areas.essence: The real line, limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration made rigorous.
areas.description: Real analysis studies the real line and functions on it. It gives rigorous foundations to limits, continuity, differentiation, integration, and the convergence of sequences and series.

areas.name: Complex Analysis
areas.essence: Functions of a complex variable: holomorphy, contour integration, residues.
areas.description: Complex analysis studies functions of a complex variable. Holomorphy, contour integration, residues, and analytic continuation reveal a rigidity and geometry absent from the real case.

areas.name: Functional Analysis
areas.essence: Infinite-dimensional function spaces with linear and topological structure.
areas.description: Functional analysis studies infinite-dimensional vector spaces of functions. It combines linear algebra with topology and analysis to treat operators, functionals, and convergence in abstract spaces.

areas.name: Measure Theory
areas.essence: Size, length, and integral generalized to arbitrary sets.
areas.description: Measure theory generalizes size, length, and integral to arbitrary sets. It provides the foundation for integration, probability, and the rigorous treatment of limiting processes.

areas.name: Differential Equations
areas.essence: Change represented by equations relating a function to its derivatives.
areas.description: Differential equations represent change by equations relating a function to its derivatives. They model how a system evolves from its current state and its local rate of change.

areas.name: Dynamical Systems
areas.essence: Change represented as a state space and a transition rule.
areas.description: Dynamical systems represent change as a state space and a transition rule. Orbits, fixed points, stability, bifurcations, and chaos describe the long-run behaviour of iterated or continuous evolution.

areas.name: Harmonic Analysis
areas.essence: Functions decomposed into waves and frequencies.
areas.description: Harmonic analysis decomposes functions into waves and frequencies. Fourier series, Fourier transforms, and wavelets represent a function by its spectral content.

areas.name: Probability
areas.essence: Uncertainty encoded as a measure over outcomes, with rules for combining and updating.
areas.description: Probability encodes uncertainty as a measure over outcomes. It supplies the rules for combining, conditioning, and updating beliefs or frequencies.

areas.name: Statistics
areas.essence: Inference from data: estimation, testing, and decision under uncertainty.
areas.description: Statistics draws inference from data under uncertainty. Estimation, hypothesis testing, and decision theory connect probability models to observations.

areas.name: Information Theory
areas.essence: Uncertainty and communication encoded as entropy and channel capacity.
areas.description: Information theory encodes uncertainty and communication as entropy, mutual information, and channel capacity. It studies the limits of compression and reliable transmission.

areas.name: Game Theory
areas.essence: Strategic interaction represented by players, strategies, and payoffs.
areas.description: Game theory represents strategic interaction by players, strategies, and payoffs. It studies equilibrium, cooperation, and the logic of interdependent decisions.

areas.name: Numerical Analysis
areas.essence: Continuous problems approximated by finite, computable procedures.
areas.description: Numerical analysis approximates continuous problems by finite, computable procedures. It studies discretization, iterative methods, error, stability, and convergence.

areas.name: Optimization
areas.essence: Extremal problems: the best element under constraints.
areas.description: Optimization studies extremal problems: finding the best element under constraints. It combines analysis, linear algebra, and algorithms to characterize and compute minima and maxima.

areas.name: Algorithms
areas.essence: Effective procedures and their resources: what can be computed, at what cost.
areas.description: The theory of algorithms studies effective procedures and their resources. It asks what can be computed, at what cost, and with what guarantees.

areas.name: Proof
areas.essence: The construction of warranted conclusions: inference from premises to a conclusion.
areas.description: Proof is the construction of warranted conclusions. It selects the inference rules, assumptions, and constructions that make a conclusion follow, and it is the standard by which mathematical claims are accepted.

areas.name: Approximation
areas.essence: Replacing an intractable object by a tractable one, with a controlled error.
areas.description: Approximation replaces an intractable object by a tractable one while controlling the error. It is the common move behind numerical methods, asymptotic analysis, perturbation, and discretization.

areas.name: Reduction
areas.essence: Transforming a problem into another whose solution yields the original.
areas.description: Reduction transforms a problem into another whose solution yields the original. It is the standard way to transfer a result, an algorithm, or a difficulty from one area to another.

areas.name: Symmetry
areas.essence: Invariance under transformation: the same structure seen from a different frame.
areas.description: Symmetry is invariance under transformation. It identifies the changes that leave a structure unchanged, and it turns that invariance into a tool for classification and reduction.

areas.name: Duality
areas.essence: Two descriptions of the same structure, each making a different property visible.
areas.description: Duality gives two descriptions of the same structure, each making a different property visible. It is a method of translation: a problem in one description becomes a possibly easier problem in the other.
